evidence.excerpt: Moat-type splits in ground planes, often introduced to isolate analogue and digital regions, are known to increase radiated emissions when high-frequency signals cross them. This study quantifies the effect using method-of-moments modelling of a canonical two-layer board geometry with a 50 Ω microstrip carrying a 200 MHz square-wave clock. Moat widths of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, and 2.0 mm were evaluated with and without a 100 nF bridging capacitor placed at the crossing point. The MoM solver was validated by a controlled experiment in a GTEM cell. Without bridging, a 1 mm moat increased the peak radiated electric field at CISPR class B limits by 7.4 dB at the third harmonic (600 MHz). A single bridging capacitor reduced the excess to 1.8 dB. These results are mapped onto a simple analytical expression involving crossing current, moat length, and frequency, allowing designers to estimate the penalty before committing to layout. Limitations of the analytical approximation above 800 MHz are discussed.
